name: Adam Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Adam Ito, 27, and I’m a senior lineworker who leads a crew when the supervisor is away. We meet at the west service yard, check the switching sheet, and drive out to repair distribution lines; I’m usually the one who asks for a second look if a plan feels rushed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about the work, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like work you can point to at the end of a shift, like a repaired span and a town with power again. The weather and overtime wear me out, but my pay is typical for the job and I’ve saved a few months of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a small program can format the maintenance notes, but it cannot look up a pole and tell whether the crossarm is split. We still need a worker to check the line and sign the permit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our crew work stays much as it is, and maybe the office finishes its notes earlier. I don’t expect a big change to my wage in this picture, and my savings give me some room for a car problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d let the office trial the note program but check the finished permit against our paper copy before the crew leaves. I’d keep the same work routine and leave my savings alone unless the van or home needs a repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm because I don’t see this small tool taking the field work. I still don’t want a machine’s neat notes mistaken for a safety check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the computer left out a switching step?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stop the crew from using the permit and call the control room to confirm the sequence. Then I’d write the missing step on the copy we carry in the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your usual savings plan because of this small change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I’d keep my regular transfer and not spend money on a new tool just because the office has one. My cushion is there for a real problem, not for chasing every update.

say: I’d say a program can format **maintenance notes**, but a worker checks the pole.
I’d keep the **permit and switching steps** under human review.
think: I think our **crew work stays steady** in this small-change picture.
I don’t expect a major wage change, and my **savings provide some room**.
do: Check the **digital permit** against the paper copy before dispatch.
Keep my **normal work routine** and savings plan.
Call the **control room** if a switching step is missing.
feel: I feel **calm about my job**, though I still insist on safe checks.
S0.quote: I still don’t want a machine’s neat notes mistaken for a safety check.
fieldNote: Adam trusts **paper verification** and distinguishes formatted notes from inspection at a real job site.
His **moderate savings cushion** makes this small change feel manageable.

steps.text: Check digital permits against the paper copy before dispatch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the computer can sort work orders and supply lists, but it must not bypass the crew’s site inspection. I’d ask management to show us exactly how the system handles the switching sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I help with planning when I lead, so some of those duties could shrink. I think the physical side lasts longer, but if the company needs fewer leads, my years on the line may not protect my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the supervisor to run the system beside our existing checklist before we rely on it. I’d keep my inspection skills current and put a few extra hours of pay into savings while I watch whether staffing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy because planning is part of my lead work, but there is time to see what the company does. My savings give me a little breathing space, not enough to ignore a cut in hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need before trusting the system with a work order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want it tested against real faults and signed off by a qualified person who knows the service area. A sales demonstration at the depot would not convince me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the planning duty disappears, would you assume a field vacancy will be waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn’t assume the company has an open field slot or that another utility is hiring. I’d ask about actual hours and vacancies before I made a move.

say: I’d say software can sort **orders and supplies**, but crews must inspect sites.
I’d ask to see how the system handles the **switching sheet**.
think: I think my **planning duties could shrink** when I lead.
I think my line experience may not protect my **paid hours** if fewer leads are needed.
do: Test the new system beside the **existing checklist** before relying on it.
Keep inspection skills current and **save overtime pay**.
Ask about **actual hours and vacancies** before considering a move.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, since a small cushion cannot absorb a lasting cut.
S1.quote: I think the physical side lasts longer, but if the company needs fewer leads, my years on the line may not protect my hours.
fieldNote: He sees exposure in **lead planning duties** and asks how staffing may change.
His caution is practical: he asks for **field-tested evidence**, not a sales demonstration.

steps.text: Test the dispatch system beside the existing checklist
Save a portion of overtime pay
Wait for verified staffing and vacancy information before applying elsewhere

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say scheduling, records and fault diagnosis are all exposed after 2028, so no one should call the lead desk work permanent. The crew has a gap before robots arrive in 2031, but I would expect the company to plan for that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the company could cut lead posts first, and later robots could take some physical line work. I have a few months saved, which helps, but I don’t know whether there will be another job nearby when that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask about an electrical safety trainer certificate and use the two years to complete the parts that require a real instructor. In 2029 I’d apply to open trainer posts, but I would check how much is hands-on because planning and diagnosis are not safe careers after AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because I expect the company to need fewer people in my role, and the local choices are limited. My savings give me a short runway, not an answer about what I earn afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your savings if the company announced a restructuring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep enough for rent and bills first, and avoid spending it on a course until I knew the terms. I’d ask the supervisor whether training time is paid and whether any post is actually budgeted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You’ve named trainer work, but its lesson planning is thinking work. Could it be protected after full AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can’t call training protected after 2028 because the system could write lessons and answer questions. I’d check whether a practical instructor vacancy exists, while accepting it could also disappear.

say: I’d say scheduling and diagnosis are **exposed after 2028**, not permanent jobs.
I’d expect the company to plan for the **2031 robot date**.
think: I think **lead jobs may shrink**, with physical work exposed later.
I don’t know whether **local vacancies** will take my skills.
do: Ask about an **electrical safety trainer certificate** now.
Apply to actual trainer openings in **2029** and check hands-on duties.
Protect **rent money** and verify whether training time is paid.
feel: I feel **anxious about fewer jobs**, though my savings buy some time.
S2.quote: My savings give me a short runway, not an answer about what I earn afterward.
fieldNote: Adam expects job reductions and sees **limited local alternatives**, while using savings as a buffer.
He tests training options but refuses to treat **instructor work as protected**.

steps.text: Ask about a practical electrical safety trainer certificate
Apply to budgeted trainer vacancies in 2029 after reviewing duties
Keep savings available for rent and household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years lets us check training and staffing instead of reacting in a rush. It does not make records or diagnosis safe after 2031, and the robot date still reaches physical line work in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can plan more carefully and build my savings before the change, which matters more than getting excited about a new course. I still expect lead duties to be reduced, though I can’t say how many people will lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for a written list of qualifications the company will recognize and start with a paid safety course. In 2032 I’d compare real instructor vacancies and keep enough savings for a deposit if a job required moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but I have time to get facts and build a more useful reserve. Five years is not so long that I can put off deciding until the last month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you believe the training is worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want the company to name the qualification and show open posts that use it. I’d ask someone who finished the course what the work was like before I gave up overtime for class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a suitable vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d consider it if the pay covers the extra rent and travel and Mina wants the move too. I have some savings, but I would not leave a steady wage for a verbal promise.

say: I’d say five years gives us time to check **training and staffing**.
I wouldn’t call records safe after 2031 or line work safe after **2034**.
think: I can build savings and plan **more carefully** before the change.
I expect **lead duties to shrink**, though I don’t know how many jobs go.
do: Get a written list of **recognized qualifications** and start a paid course.
Keep enough savings for a **moving deposit** if an offer requires relocation.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but I can prepare while checking the facts.
S3.quote: Five years is not so long that I can put off deciding until the last month.
fieldNote: He uses the warning to **verify credentials and vacancies**, not chase novelty.
His moderate savings cushion gives choices, while **relocation costs** and Mina’s wishes still matter.

steps.text: Start a paid safety course the company recognizes
Build savings while continuing the current lineworker job
Compare instructor vacancies in 2032 and review the pay
Move only if the offer covers costs and Mina agrees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years is long enough to prepare in steps, but nobody should promise that a crew job lasts forever. We should know what happens to the records and lead work by 2036, and to field work by 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could finish a safety qualification, build my savings, and check the job market without giving up my current wage too early. I would not count on trainer work as safe because lesson writing and diagnosis are thinking work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take a recognized course in smaller blocks and keep my savings transfer going until I had three months of bills. In 2037 I’d apply to instructor jobs only after checking their duties and the employer’s pay offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed than with a two-year warning, and my savings give me a little control. I still worry that a steady income could end before I find work that fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mina see you change this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She’d see me protect our regular savings transfer and put a few evenings into the course. We’d stay in our current place until a real job offer made a move sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could an instructor or inspection role be a permanently safe career after AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, those roles use planning and records that AI can do too. I’d treat them as possible work to investigate, not as a lifetime guarantee.

I’d ask about records by 2036 and **field work by 2039**.
think: I can qualify and save while keeping my **current wage**.
I won’t call trainer work **permanently safe**, since it includes exposed thinking tasks.
do: Take a recognized **safety course** in smaller blocks.
Continue saving until I have **three months** of bills.
Apply in **2037** only after checking the duties and written pay.
feel: I feel **less rushed**, but I still worry about losing steady income.
S4.quote: I would not count on trainer work as safe because lesson writing and diagnosis are thinking work too.
fieldNote: A longer lead time encourages **measured preparation**, but does not make job protection permanent.
He connects a move to **verified pay** and agreement from Mina.

steps.text: Take a recognized electrical safety course in smaller blocks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the thinking tasks change quickly and robots follow in 2031. Paid training with a recognized qualification, written information about any staffing change, and time to use my savings carefully would help me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the safety procedure when a computer updates a work order. A lineworker should be able to explain what changed before a crew is sent out to use it.

headlineQuote: A lineworker should be able to explain what changed before a crew is sent out to use it.
portrait: Adam is a **senior lineworker** who values careful repairs and visible results.
He earns typical pay and has **a few months saved**, more cushion than many workers.
He prefers **proven tools** and written procedures before changing how crews work.
He plans to **train and save** while recognizing that desk work and field work face different timelines.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** changes thinking tasks quickly, with robots following in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid recognized training**, written staffing information and time to use his savings carefully would help.
